channel.title: A trainer’s field notes
channel.description: Short pieces on training, writing and AI adoption by Annamalai Muthiah.

item.title: Useful metrics. Not the point.
item.description: Attendance, completion, certification and a great feedback score prove the training happened. They don’t show whether people use what they learned.

item.title: You bought the AI tools. Now what?
item.description: Eight lessons on getting people to actually use the AI tools their company already paid for.

item.title: The companies “behind” on AI might have the easier road
item.description: Why teams with fewer technical people often have more to gain from AI, and nine ways a writer and trainer helps them get there.
item.content:encoded:
Most AI rollouts I’ve seen stall in the same place. The license gets bought, the launch email goes out, there’s a demo with a lot of applause. Then Monday comes and people go back to working the way they always have.

The tool was fine. Nobody showed them where it fit in their actual day.

I’ve spent over 20 years writing documentation and running training programs, and I keep coming back to one idea. Companies with fewer technical people often have more to gain from AI, and a clearer path to getting there, if someone does the translation work.

Why the less technical company has an edge

  • The gains are bigger and easier to see. When someone spends two hours a week formatting reports, saving that time is obvious. Nobody needs a dashboard to prove it.
  • There are fewer bad habits to undo. Tech-heavy teams often already have a mess of personal tools, random prompts, and “shadow AI” nobody approved. A fresh start is easier to shape.
  • People ask honest questions. “Will this replace me?” “What if I type something wrong?” Those questions are gold for a trainer. They tell you exactly what to address.
  • One good process spreads fast. In a smaller or less technical team, a single workflow that works gets copied by word of mouth.

Where a writer and trainer actually helps

  1. Start with the work. Before touching any tool, I’d sit with teams and list the tasks that eat their week. Emails, summaries, meeting notes, first drafts, FAQs. AI adoption begins with a boring spreadsheet of real tasks.
  2. Translate the jargon. “LLM,” “prompt,” “hallucination,” “agent.” Most people nod along and understand none of it. A one-page plain-language glossary does more for adoption than a keynote.
  3. Say the fear out loud. People worry about their jobs and about looking stupid. I’d name both in the first session. Pretending the fear isn’t there makes it louder.
  4. Pick one small win. One team, one task, one week. Show the before and after. A single believable result beats a big vision deck every time.
  5. Write the prompts for them. Most people freeze at a blank chat box. I’d build a starter library of prompts tied to their real templates and documents. Copy, paste, adjust. Confidence comes later.
  6. Make the rules simple. What data can go in, what can’t, and who to ask when unsure. If the policy reads like a legal contract, people will either ignore it or avoid the tool entirely.
  7. Train in short bursts. Fifteen minutes, one skill, practiced on their own work. Then a job aid they can pin next to their screen. The three-hour webinar is where adoption goes to die.
  8. Grow champions inside the team. Find the two or three curious people in each department and give them extra support. Peers are more convincing than any trainer.
  9. Measure what matters to people. Hours saved, yes. Also ask how they feel about using it. Confidence is the real leading indicator.

What changes next

The tools will keep shifting. Today it’s chat assistants, and agents that take actions on your behalf are already arriving. Whatever training we build now will need refreshing every few months.

What won’t change is the need for someone who can look at a new tool, understand the people using it, and explain the connection in plain words. That’s been the writer’s and trainer’s job all along. AI just raised the stakes.

If you’re leading a team that feels “behind” on AI, you might be closer than you think. You don’t need more tools. You need someone to walk your people through the first few steps.

What’s the biggest thing holding your team back from using AI day to day? I’d genuinely like to know.
